analysis.one_liner: Banned commercial harvest of Atlantic striped bass in coastal waters and federal waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Resources Committee's fisheries subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would outlaw commercial fishing for Atlantic striped bass in state coastal waters and the federal exclusive economic zone, with civil fines up to $1,000 per violation and forfeiture of vessels and catch for violators. It would require the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission to amend its management plan and the Fish and Wildlife Service to adjust its striped bass study accordingly. The goal is to conserve the species by ending commercial harvest, leaving striped bass primarily to recreational anglers.
analysis.who_benefits: Recreational anglers and coastal communities whose economies depend on sportfishing for striped bass, plus the general public interested in the species' recovery and long-term abundance.

how_it_helps.text: It makes commercial harvesting of Atlantic striped bass unlawful in coastal waters and the exclusive economic zone [S3].
It imposes civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation and allows forfeiture of vessels, gear, and catch used in violations, deterring illegal harvest [S3].
It directs the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission to amend its striped bass management plan to reflect the ban and the Fish and Wildlife Service to adjust its study scope [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial fishermen who harvest Atlantic striped bass would lose a source of catch and income, and consumers could face changes in the supply of wild striped bass.

drawbacks.text: The bill's penalties are relatively light: a civil penalty capped at $1,000 per violation [S3].
A full commercial ban eliminates lawful commercial fishing for the species, ending an existing fishery rather than managing it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear conservation gain for a popular sport fish at the cost of eliminating commercial harvest, a trade-off its sponsor judged worthwhile; its effectiveness as drafted was limited by modest penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Resources Committee, which sent it to the fisheries subcommittee; no hearing or vote ever occurred before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 1999 and referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day [S5].
On March 10, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans and executive comment was requested from the Commerce Department [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial striped bass fishermen kept their existing fishery, since no restriction took effect; the species' management continued under existing law unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Commercial fishermen, unaffected by the inaction

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban commercial striped bass harvest [S1].

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never advanced the bill to the full House [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its subcommittee referral without action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no partisan breakdown exists [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end their harvest in coastal and federal waters, enforced by fines and vessel forfeiture [S3].
More abundant striped bass would benefit anglers and the businesses that serve them.
Wild striped bass supply could shrink, though the species' recovery could support the fishery long term.
